direct_claims: This chart reports results from a task-based usability test with 11 interpretive tasks.
The figure is from a paper published at CHI in 2021.
Each percentage represents the share of participants who were able to partially or fully succeed in completing a task.
The tasks concern interpreting objects and relationships on a pre-made slide, including object identification, color, width, position, relative size, arrow direction, and text-box content.
Because the caption counts both partial and full success together, these values should be interpreted as an upper-bound measure of usable performance rather than a measure of perfect understanding.
These results matter because they identify which kinds of interpretive tasks users could and could not complete in the tested system.
derived_claims: Performance varies widely across tasks, from 0.0% to 91.7%. — derived by reading the minimum and maximum percentages from the provided task list.

The highest-success tasks are identifying objects on the pre-made slide at 91.7% and identifying the text in the text box at 90.9%. — derived by ranking tasks by percentage from the provided task list.

The lowest-success task is determining the direction the arrow is pointing at 0.0%, indicating complete failure on that task in this sample. — derived by identifying the minimum value from the provided task list.

Overall, participants appear to do much better on basic object or text identification than on spatial-relation or directional interpretation tasks. — derived by comparing high-performing identification tasks against lower-performing relation/direction tasks across the provided task list.

Tasks involving direct recognition tend to score higher here: identifying objects is 91.7% and identifying text-box text is 90.9%. — derived by reading and comparing the listed percentages for tasks 1 and 10.

Several tasks requiring spatial reasoning are substantially lower: determining positions on the slide is 50.0% for rectangle and oval, 45.5% for arrow position, 45.5% for text-box position, and 36.4% for text-box position relative to other objects. — derived by grouping and comparing the listed percentages for spatial-position tasks.

Relative comparison tasks also appear difficult, with rectangle color at 25.0%, rectangle and oval relative position at 36.4%, and relative size at 54.5%. — derived by grouping and comparing the listed percentages for comparison/relationship tasks.

The 0.0% score for arrow direction suggests that directional encoding was especially hard for participants to recover in this study condition. — derived by interpreting the zero success rate for task 8 from the provided task list.

If a tool supports recognition of object existence and text content but not direction or spatial relationships, users may miss important meaning that depends on layout rather than labels alone. — derived by contrasting high success on object/text identification with low success on direction/relative-position tasks.

The moderate-to-low scores on relative position tasks suggest that understanding relationships among objects may remain unreliable even when individual objects can be found. — derived by comparing object-identification success with multiple lower relative-position scores.

Two tasks share the same percentage of 45.5%: determining the arrow's position on the slide and determining the text box's position on the slide. — derived by matching equal values in the provided task list.

Two tasks also share 36.4%: determining the rectangle's and oval's positions relative to each other, and determining the text box's position relative to the other objects. — derived by matching equal values in the provided task list.
Six of the eleven tasks are below 50% success. — derived by counting tasks with percentages under 50 from the provided task list.
The median task success is 45.5%. — derived by sorting the 11 percentages and selecting the middle value.
The mean success rate across all tasks is about 48.6%. — derived by averaging the 11 listed percentages.
speculative_claims: In usability research, task success percentages are commonly used to show which functions or information types users can interpret reliably and which ones create barriers. — speculative from human-computer interaction/usability research.

In accessibility and interface interpretation contexts, failures on direction and relative position often indicate that users can access object presence but not enough structural information to infer layout or relationships. — speculative from accessibility/HCI interpretation research.

For accessibility-related technologies, that gap can affect whether a person can fully understand diagrams, slides, or educational materials rather than merely detect that elements are present. — speculative from accessibility and assistive technology.

The especially poor performance on arrow direction is potentially important because arrows often encode flow, causality, sequence, or emphasis in instructional and presentation materials. — speculative from information visualization/presentation design.

If similar patterns held in broader use, designers and researchers would likely need to improve how nonvisual or usability support conveys spatial structure, direction, and inter-object relationships. — speculative from accessibility design and HCI practice.
